nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-01.title: Count 3-digit and 4-digit page numbers
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-01.body:
If all $120$ pages had 3-digit numbers there would be $360 < 417$ digits; if all had 4-digit numbers there would be $480 > 417$. So some are 3-digit and some 4-digit. Let $x$ pages have 3 digits and $y$ have 4 digits:
$$x + y = 120,\qquad 3x + 4y = 417.$$
Subtracting $3\times$ the first from the second gives $y = 57$, so $x = 63$. The 4-digit pages are $1000, 1001, \dots$, and the 57th of them is $1056$, the last page.

**Answer: 1056**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-01.title: Count extra digits
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-01.body:
Each of the $120$ pages has at least 3 digits, giving $360$; the extra $417 - 360 = 57$ digits come from the pages numbered $1000$ or more, one extra digit each. So exactly $57$ pages are numbered $1000, \dots, 1056$, and the book ends on page $1056$. (Check: pages $937$–$999$ are $63$ pages with $189$ digits, plus $57 \cdot 4 = 228$, total $417$.)

**Answer: 1056**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-02.title: Split into two triangles
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-02.body:
Split $[PBCM] = [BCM] + [BPM]$.
- $\triangle BCM$ is right with legs $BC = 1$ and $CM = \frac12$, so $[BCM] = \frac14$.
- $\triangle BPM$ and $\triangle BAM$ have the same height from $B$ to line $AM$, so $\frac{[BPM]}{[BAM]} = \frac{PM}{AM}$. Here $PM = MC = \frac12$ and $AM = \sqrt{1 + \frac14} = \frac{\sqrt5}{2}$, while $[BAM] = \frac12 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = \frac12$ (base $AB$, height $1$). So $[BPM] = \frac12 \cdot \frac{1/2}{\sqrt5/2} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt5} = \frac{\sqrt5}{10}$.

Total: $\frac14 + \frac{\sqrt5}{10} = \frac{5 + 2\sqrt5}{20}$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt5+5}{20}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-02.title: Coordinates and the shoelace formula
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-02.body:
Let $A = (0,0)$, $B = (1,0)$, $C = (1,1)$, $D = (0,1)$, $M = \left(\frac12, 1\right)$. Moving from $M$ toward $A$ a distance $\frac12$ along $AM$ (length $\frac{\sqrt5}{2}$) gives $P = M - \frac{1}{\sqrt5}\left(\frac12, 1\right) = \left(\frac12 - \frac{1}{2\sqrt5},\ 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt5}\right)$.

Shoelace for $P, B, C, M$:
$$2[PBCM] = |x_P y_B - x_B y_P + x_B y_C - x_C y_B + x_C y_M - x_M y_C + x_M y_P - x_P y_M|.$$
This is $\left|-\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\right) + 1 + \left(1 - \tfrac12\right) + \tfrac12\left(1 - \tfrac1{\sqrt5}\right) - \left(\tfrac12 - \tfrac1{2\sqrt5}\right)\right| = \tfrac12 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$, so the area is $\frac14 + \frac{1}{2\sqrt5} = \frac{5 + 2\sqrt5}{20} \approx 0.4736$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt5+5}{20}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-03.title: Assume a ≤ b and test small a
Parity shortcut
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-03.body:
$2530$ is even, so $a^b$ and $b^a$ have the same parity, i.e. $a$ and $b$ have the same parity. If both were even, both terms would be divisible by $4$ (each base is even and each exponent is at least $2$, except when an exponent is $1$, which can't happen since both are even), but $2530 \equiv 2 \pmod 4$. So both are odd. With $a \le b$ odd: $a = 1$ gives $b = 2529$; $a = 3$ needs $3^b + b^3 = 2530$, and $b = 7$ works ($2187 + 343$); $a = 5$ is already too big. Including swaps, the values of $a$ are $1, 3, 7, 2529$, summing to $2540$.

**Answer: 2540**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-04.title: Factor out the gcd
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-04.body:
Let $g = \gcd(x, y)$, $x = ga$, $y = gb$ with $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ and $a < b$. Then $\operatorname{lcm}(x,y) = gab$, so the condition is $ab = 2024 = 2^3 \cdot 11 \cdot 23$. Since $a, b$ are coprime, each prime power goes entirely into $a$ or $b$:
$$(a, b) \in \{(1, 2024),\ (8, 253),\ (11, 184),\ (23, 88)\}.$$
We need $y = gb \le 2024$, i.e. $g \le \frac{2024}{b}$: that allows $1, 8, 11, 23$ values of $g$ respectively. Total $1 + 8 + 11 + 23 = 43$.

**Answer: 43**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-04.title: Count via the smaller factor
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-04.body:
Notice that $\frac{2024}{b} = a$ in each case above, so the number of choices of $g$ equals $a$. Hence the answer is the sum of the smaller element $a$ over all ways to split $2024$ into a coprime product $ab$ with $a < b$. The $2^3 = 8$ coprime ordered splittings pair up into $4$ unordered ones, with smaller parts $1, 8, 11, 23$, summing to $43$. A brute-force check over all pairs $x < y \le 2024$ also gives $43$.

**Answer: 43**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-05.title: Place the rooks one at a time
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-05.body:
Place the rooks in order. The first can go anywhere. The second must avoid the first rook's row and column: $7 \cdot 7 = 49$ good squares out of the $63$ remaining. The third must avoid two rows and two columns: $6 \cdot 6 = 36$ good squares out of $62$. So
$$P = \frac{49}{63} \cdot \frac{36}{62} = \frac79 \cdot \frac{18}{31} = \frac{14}{31}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{14}{31}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-05.title: Count sets of squares
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-05.body:
Total ways to choose 3 squares: $\binom{64}{3} = 41664$. Non-attacking: choose 3 rows ($\binom83 = 56$), 3 columns ($56$), and match them up ($3! = 6$): $56 \cdot 56 \cdot 6 = 18816$. Probability $\frac{18816}{41664} = \frac{14}{31}$.

**Answer: $\frac{14}{31}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-06.title: Factor out the fixed points
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-06.body:
Expanding, $f(f(x)) - x = x^4 - 40x^3 + 428x^2 - 561x + 120$, a quartic with no rational roots. But every solution of $f(x) = x$ also solves $f(f(x)) = x$, so $f(x) - x = x^2 - 21x + 24$ divides the quartic. Dividing:
$$x^4 - 40x^3 + 428x^2 - 561x + 120 = (x^2 - 21x + 24)(x^2 - 19x + 5).$$
The quadratic formula gives $x = \frac{21 \pm \sqrt{441 - 96}}{2} = \frac{21 \pm \sqrt{345}}{2}$ and $x = \frac{19 \pm \sqrt{361 - 20}}{2} = \frac{19 \pm \sqrt{341}}{2}$, all real.

**Answer: $\frac{21 \pm \sqrt{345}}{2}$ and $\frac{19 \pm \sqrt{341}}{2}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-06.title: Use 2-cycles
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-06.body:
Besides fixed points, solutions of $f(f(x)) = x$ come in pairs $x \ne y$ with $f(x) = y$, $f(y) = x$. Subtracting $y = x^2 - 20x + 24$ and $x = y^2 - 20y + 24$:
$$y - x = (x^2 - y^2) - 20(x - y) \implies -1 = (x + y) - 20 \implies x + y = 19.$$
Adding them: $x + y = x^2 + y^2 - 20(x+y) + 48$, so $x^2 + y^2 = 19 + 380 - 48 = 351$ and $xy = \frac{19^2 - 351}{2} = 5$. So $x, y$ are the roots of $t^2 - 19t + 5$: $\frac{19 \pm \sqrt{341}}{2}$. Together with the fixed points $\frac{21 \pm\sqrt{345}}{2}$ (roots of $x^2 - 21x + 24$), these are all four solutions.

**Answer: $\frac{21 \pm \sqrt{345}}{2}$ and $\frac{19 \pm \sqrt{341}}{2}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-07.title: List the values
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-07.body:
The divisor counts of $1, 2, \dots, 10$ are $1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 4, 2, 4, 3, 4$, whose sum is $27$.

**Answer: 27**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-07.title: Count by divisor
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-07.body:
Each $d$ from $1$ to $10$ divides $\lfloor 10/d \rfloor$ of the numbers $1, \dots, 10$. So the sum is
$$10 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 27.$$

**Answer: 27**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-08.title: Stars and bars
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-08.body:
Say the chosen N is in the $n$-th copy of NYC, the Y in the $y$-th copy and the C in the $c$-th copy. Within a copy N comes before Y before C, so the selection is in order exactly when $1 \le n \le y \le c \le 6$. The number of such non-decreasing triples is the number of multisets of size 3 from 6 values:
$$\binom{6 + 3 - 1}{3} = \binom83 = 56.$$

**Answer: 56**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-08.title: Sum over the Y
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-08.body:
If the Y is in copy $y$, there are $y$ choices of an N before it (copies $1, \dots, y$) and $7 - y$ choices of a C after it (copies $y, \dots, 6$). Summing:
$$\sum_{y=1}^{6} y(7-y) = 6 + 10 + 12 + 12 + 10 + 6 = 56.$$

**Answer: 56**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-10.title: Heights and parallel lines
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-10.body:
Scale so $BC = 2$, let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and assume first that $P$ is closer to $B$. Since $A$, $P$, $Q$ are collinear with $AP = 2PQ$, the distance from $Q$ to line $BC$ is half the distance from $A$, i.e. $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Also $MQ = 1$ (radius). So $\sin\angle BMQ = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and, with $P$ nearer $B$, $\angle BMQ = 60^\circ$.

Then $MQ$ makes a $60^\circ$ angle with $BC$, just like $AB$ does on the other side, so $MQ \parallel AB$. Triangles $PBA$ and $PMQ$ are similar with ratio $AB : MQ = 2 : 1$, so $BP = 2\,PM$. With $BP + PM = BM = 1$ we get $BP = \frac23$, $CP = \frac43$, and $\frac{BP}{CP} = \frac12$. By symmetry $P$ nearer $C$ gives $\frac{BP}{CP} = 2$. The sum is $\frac52$.

**Answer: $\frac52$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-10.title: Coordinates
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-10.body:
Put $B = (-1, 0)$, $C = (1, 0)$, $A = (0, \sqrt3)$, with the semicircle below $BC$, and $P = (p, 0)$. Since $Q$ is beyond $P$ with $PQ = \frac12 AP$, $Q = P + \frac12(P - A) = \left(\frac{3p}{2}, -\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Requiring $|Q| = 1$: $\frac{9p^2}{4} + \frac34 = 1$, so $p = \pm\frac13$. Then $\frac{BP}{CP} = \frac{1 + p}{1 - p} = 2$ or $\frac12$, summing to $\frac52$.

**Answer: $\frac52$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-11.title: Average the vowel fractions
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-11.body:
Each word is chosen with probability $\frac14$, so the answer is the average of the vowel fractions: YOU $\frac23$, BELONG $\frac26$, WITH $\frac14$, ME $\frac12$.
$$\frac14\left(\frac23 + \frac13 + \frac14 + \frac12\right) = \frac14 \cdot \frac74 = \frac{7}{16}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{7}{16}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-11.title: Common denominator
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-11.body:
Give each word $12$ equally likely tickets, split evenly among its letters: YOU gives $8$ vowel tickets of $12$, BELONG $4$, WITH $3$, ME $6$. Out of $48$ tickets, $8 + 4 + 3 + 6 = 21$ are vowels, so the probability is $\frac{21}{48} = \frac{7}{16}$.

**Answer: $\frac{7}{16}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-12.title: Count lattice points under a hyperbola
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-12.body:
$\tau(n)$ counts the pairs $(i, j)$ of positive integers with $ij = n$, so the sum counts all pairs with $ij \le 100$, i.e. lattice points in the first quadrant under $xy = 100$. The region is symmetric about $y = x$. Points with $i \le 10$ plus points with $j \le 10$ count every point at least once (if $i, j > 10$ then $ij > 100$), and the $10 \times 10$ square of points with both $\le 10$ is counted twice. Points with $i \le 10$:
$$\sum_{i=1}^{10}\left\lfloor \frac{100}{i}\right\rfloor = 100 + 50 + 33 + 25 + 20 + 16 + 14 + 12 + 11 + 10 = 291.$$
So the total is $2 \cdot 291 - 100 = 482$.

**Answer: 482**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-12.title: Count by divisor
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-12.body:
Each $d \le 100$ divides $\lfloor 100/d \rfloor$ numbers up to $100$, so the sum is $\sum_{d=1}^{100}\lfloor 100/d\rfloor$. Grouping equal values: $d = 1..10$ give $291$ (as listed above); $d = 11$ gives $9$; $12$ gives $8$; $13,14$ give $7$ each; $15,16$ give $6$; $17$–$20$ give $5$; $21$–$25$ give $4$; $26$–$33$ give $3$; $34$–$50$ give $2$; $51$–$100$ give $1$. Total: $291 + 9 + 8 + 14 + 12 + 20 + 20 + 24 + 34 + 50 = 482$.

**Answer: 482**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-13.title: Use the middle term
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-13.body:
The second-largest angle is three steps after the smallest, so the common difference is $\frac{(155 - x) - (5x - 58)}{3} = 71 - 2x$. The middle angle is $155 - x - (71 - 2x) = 84 + x$. The angles sum to $540^\circ$, so the middle (average) angle is $108^\circ$: $84 + x = 108$, $x = 24$. The common difference is $71 - 48 = 23$, so the largest angle is $108 + 2 \cdot 23 = 154^\circ$.

**Answer: $154^\circ$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-13.title: Two equations
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-13.body:
Let the angles be $a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, a + 4d$. Then $5a + 10d = 540$ (so $a + 2d = 108$), $a = 5x - 58$ and $a + 3d = 155 - x$. From the last two, $3d = 213 - 6x$, so $d = 71 - 2x$, and $a + 2d = 5x - 58 + 142 - 4x = x + 84 = 108$, giving $x = 24$, $a = 62$, $d = 23$. Angles $62, 85, 108, 131, 154$ (sum $540$ ✓). Largest: $154^\circ$.

**Answer: $154^\circ$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-15.title: Skip blocks
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-15.body:
Each choice of first digit gives a block of $4! = 24$ consecutive numbers. Numbers starting with 1 or 2 fill positions $1$–$48$, so the $55$th starts with $3$ and is the $7$th number in that block. Within it, each second digit gives a block of $3! = 6$: second digit $1$ covers positions $1$–$6$, so the $7$th has second digit $2$ and is the first of the numbers starting $32$, which is $32145$.

**Answer: 32145**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-15.title: Count backwards from a nearby number
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-15.body:
Numbers before $32145$: those starting with $1$ or $2$ ($48$), and those starting with $31$ ($6$). That makes $54$ numbers before it, so $32145$ is the $55$th.

**Answer: 32145**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-16.title: Minimize the distance to the origin
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-16.body:
Let $O$ be the origin. For fixed $Q$ (outside the unit circle), $PQ \ge OQ - OP = OQ - 1$, with equality when $P$ is on segment $OQ$. So we minimize $OQ$. For $Q = (a, b)$ on the curve,
$$OQ^2 = a^2 + a^4 + 4a^3 + 5a^2 + 4a + 50 = (a + 1)^4 + 49 \ge 49,$$
with equality at $a = -1$. So $OQ \ge 7$ and the minimum of $PQ$ is $7 - 1 = 6$ (at $Q = (-1, \sqrt{48})$, $P = \frac17 Q$).

**Answer: 6**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-16.title: Compare circles
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-16.body:
Every point of the curve satisfies $x^2 + y^2 = (x+1)^4 + 49 \ge 49$, so the curve lies outside (or on) the circle of radius $7$ about $O$, touching it at $(-1, \sqrt{48})$. The gap between the circles of radius $1$ and $7$ is $6$, and it is attained along the ray through the touching point. So the minimum distance is $6$.

**Answer: 6**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-17.title: Triangle inequality
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-17.body:
Let the two sides be $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\varepsilon + 19$, and the third side $s$. The triangle inequality gives $\varepsilon + s > \varepsilon + 19$, so $s > 19$. The perimeter is $2\varepsilon + 19 + s > 0 + 19 + 19 = 38$. So the perimeter is more than $38$, and $39$ is achievable, e.g. $\varepsilon = \frac13$, sides $\frac13, \frac{58}{3}, \frac{58}{3}$ (an isosceles triangle with $\frac13 + \frac{58}{3} > \frac{58}{3}$). ✓

**Answer: 39**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-17.title: Think of degenerate triangles
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-17.body:
Take the thin isosceles triangles with sides $\varepsilon$, $19 + \varepsilon$, $19 + \varepsilon$: two sides differ by $19$, and the perimeter is $38 + 3\varepsilon$, which can be any number above $38$. Nothing smaller is possible: the longer of the two special sides, $\varepsilon + 19$, is less than the sum of the other two, so the perimeter exceeds $2(\varepsilon + 19) > 38$. With $\varepsilon = \frac13$ the perimeter is $39$, the smallest integer above $38$.

**Answer: 39**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-18.title: Compare the inradii
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-18.body:
Let $I_1, I_2$ be the incenters of $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle ACD$, with inradii $r_1, r_2$, and let $E, F$ be their feet on $BC$. Since $DI_1$ and $DI_2$ bisect the right angles at $D$, $DE = r_1$ and $DF = r_2$, so $EF = r_1 + r_2$. The angle $\theta$ between $I_1I_2$ and $BC$ satisfies
$$\tan\theta = \frac{r_1 - r_2}{r_1 + r_2}.$$
Note $\angle A = 90^\circ$, so $\triangle DBA \sim \triangle DAC$ with ratio $\frac{AB}{AC} = \tan C$; hence $\frac{r_1}{r_2} = \tan C$ and
$$\tan\theta = \frac{\tan C - 1}{\tan C + 1} = \frac{\tan C - \tan 45^\circ}{1 + \tan C \tan 45^\circ} = \tan(C - 45^\circ).$$
So $\theta = 72^\circ - 45^\circ = 27^\circ$.

**Answer: $27^\circ$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-18.title: Angle chase with a similar right triangle
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-18.body:
$\angle I_1DI_2 = 45^\circ + 45^\circ = 90^\circ$ and $\frac{DI_1}{DI_2} = \frac{r_1\sqrt2}{r_2\sqrt2} = \frac{AB}{AC}$. So right triangle $I_1DI_2$ (right angle at $D$) has legs in the ratio $AB : AC$, like right triangle $BAC$ (right angle at $A$). Hence they are similar, and $\angle DI_1I_2 = \angle ABC = 18^\circ$ (both are opposite the leg corresponding to $AC$).

Since $r_1 > r_2$, line $I_1I_2$ slopes down toward $C$ and meets line $BC$ at a point $Y$ beyond $D$ on the $C$ side. In $\triangle I_1DY$: $\angle I_1 = 18^\circ$ and $\angle I_1DY = 180^\circ - 45^\circ = 135^\circ$, so $\angle Y = 180^\circ - 18^\circ - 135^\circ = 27^\circ$.

**Answer: $27^\circ$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-19.title: Side of the triangle
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-19.body:
The centers of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are $2$ apart (external tangency), so the equilateral triangle has side $2$. Internal tangency means the distance from the center of $\omega_3$ to the center of $\omega_1$ is $R - 1$, so $R - 1 = 2$, $R = 3$, and the area is $9\pi$.

**Answer: $9\pi$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-19.title: Along a radius
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-19.body:
The tangency point of $\omega_1$ with $\omega_3$, the center of $\omega_1$ and the center $O$ of $\omega_3$ are collinear. So $R = (\text{distance from } O \text{ to the center of } \omega_1) + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3$, giving area $\pi \cdot 3^2 = 9\pi$.

**Answer: $9\pi$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-20.title: List the rabbit's winning sequences
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-20.body:
Write W for a rabbit win and L for a loss. The rabbit wins a game with probability $\frac14$ when behind, else $\frac12$ (and loses with $\frac34$ or $\frac12$). The sequences in which the rabbit wins:
- WWW: $\frac18$
- LWWW: $\frac12\cdot\frac14\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12 = \frac1{32}$; WLWW: $\frac1{16}$; WWLW: $\frac1{16}$
- LLWWW: $\frac12\cdot\frac34\cdot\frac14\cdot\frac14\cdot\frac12 = \frac{3}{256}$; LWLWW: $\frac12\cdot\frac14\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac14\cdot\frac12 = \frac1{128}$; LWWLW: $\frac1{64}$; WLLWW: $\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac14\cdot\frac12 = \frac1{64}$; WLWLW: $\frac1{32}$; WWLLW: $\frac1{32}$

Sum: $\frac{32 + 8 + 16 + 16 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 8 + 8}{256} = \frac{101}{256}$.

**Answer: $\frac{101}{256}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-20.title: Recursion on the score
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-20.body:
Let $p(r, h)$ be the probability the rabbit wins from score $r$–$h$. Then $p(3, h) = 1$, $p(r, 3) = 0$, and $p(r,h) = q\,p(r+1,h) + (1-q)\,p(r,h+1)$ with $q = \frac14$ if $h > r$, else $q = \frac12$. Working backwards:
- $p(2,2) = \frac12$, $p(2,1) = \frac34$, $p(1,2) = \frac14 \cdot \frac12 = \frac18$, $p(2,0) = \frac78$, $p(0,2) = \frac14\cdot\frac18 = \frac1{32}$.
- $p(1,1) = \frac12\left(\frac34 + \frac18\right) = \frac7{16}$, $p(1,0) = \frac12\left(\frac78 + \frac7{16}\right) = \frac{21}{32}$, $p(0,1) = \frac14\cdot\frac7{16} + \frac34\cdot\frac1{32} = \frac{17}{128}$.
- $p(0,0) = \frac12\left(\frac{21}{32} + \frac{17}{128}\right) = \frac12 \cdot \frac{101}{128} = \frac{101}{256}$.

**Answer: $\frac{101}{256}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-21.title: Symmetry and a fixed point
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-21.body:
$f(x) = (x - 5)^2 + 3$ is symmetric about $x = 5$, so $f(1) = f(9) = 19$ and hence $g(1) = g(9)$. Also $f(4) = 1 + 3 = 4$, so $4$ is a fixed point and $g(4) = 4$. Therefore $g(1) + g(4) - g(9) = 4$.

**Answer: 4**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-21.title: Just the needed pieces
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-21.body:
We never need the huge value $g(1)$: since $f(1) = 1 - 10 + 28 = 19$ and $f(9) = 81 - 90 + 28 = 19$, the inputs $1$ and $9$ give identical results after the first step, so $g(1) - g(9) = 0$. And $f(4) = 16 - 40 + 28 = 4$, so $g(4) = 4$. The answer is $4$.

**Answer: 4**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-22.title: Compute OX two ways
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-22.body:
Let $M$ be the center of $S_2$, $a = AC$, $b = BC$, $r$ the radius of $\omega$ and $X$ its center. Internal tangency gives $OX = \frac{a+b}{2} - r$. Tangency to $OP$ at $P$ gives $OX^2 = OP^2 + r^2$. Since $P$ is the top of $S_2$, $MP \perp AB$, so
$$OP^2 = OM^2 + MP^2 = \left(\tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\tfrac{a}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{a^2 + b^2}{4}$$
(because $OM = OA - MA = \frac{a+b}{2} - \frac a2 = \frac b2$). Then
$$\left(\tfrac{a+b}{2} - r\right)^2 = \tfrac{a^2+b^2}{4} + r^2 \implies \tfrac{ab}{2} = r(a + b) \implies r = \frac{ab}{2(a+b)} = \frac{500}{90} = \frac{50}{9}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{50}{9}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-23.title: Square the sum of the legs
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-23.body:
With legs $a, b$: $\frac{ab}{2} = 7$ and $a^2 + b^2 = 36$. Then $(a + b)^2 = 36 + 2 \cdot 14 = 64$, so $a + b = 8$ and the perimeter is $8 + 6 = 14$.

**Answer: 14**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-23.title: Solve for the legs
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-23.body:
$a + b = s$ and $ab = 14$ with $s^2 - 28 = 36$ gives $s = 8$; the legs are the roots of $t^2 - 8t + 14 = 0$, i.e. $4 \pm \sqrt2$ (both positive, and $(4+\sqrt2)^2 + (4-\sqrt2)^2 = 36$ ✓). Perimeter $= 8 + 6 = 14$.

**Answer: 14**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-24.title: Count breakpoints with Euler's totient
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-24.body:
$f_n$ is non-decreasing on $(0,1)$ and starts at $0$. It jumps exactly at the points $\frac{m}{k}$ with $1 \le m < k \le n$, and each distinct such point increases $f_n$. So the number of values is $1 + (\text{number of distinct fractions } \tfrac mk \in (0,1) \text{ with } k \le n)$. Counting fractions by their reduced denominator $k$ gives $\varphi(k)$ new ones for each $k \ge 2$, so the number of values is $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\varphi(k)$.

Cumulative sums of $\varphi(k)$: $1, 2, 4, 6, 10, 12, 18, 22, 28, 32, 42, 46, 58$ for $k = 1, \dots, 13$. The first that reaches $50$ is at $n = 13$.

**Answer: 13**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-24.title: Check a small case and list
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-24.body:
For $n = 4$ the jump points are $\frac14, \frac13, \frac12, \frac23, \frac34$, giving $6$ values $= 1 + 1 + 2 + 2$, matching $\sum \varphi(k)$. For $n = 12$ the count is $1 + (1 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 10 + 4) = 46 < 50$, while $n = 13$ adds $\varphi(13) = 12$ new fractions to reach $58 \ge 50$. A computer count of distinct fractions confirms this.

**Answer: 13**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-25.title: Same parity
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-25.body:
The sum is even exactly when both numbers have the same parity. There are $1013$ odd and $1012$ even numbers, so
$$P = \frac{\binom{1013}{2} + \binom{1012}{2}}{\binom{2025}{2}} = \frac{1013 \cdot 1012 + 1012 \cdot 1011}{2025 \cdot 2024} = \frac{1012 \cdot 2024}{2025 \cdot 2024} = \frac{1012}{2025}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{1012}{2025}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-25.title: Condition on the first number
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-25.body:
Pick the numbers one after the other. If the first is odd (probability $\frac{1013}{2025}$), the second must be one of the other $1012$ odd numbers out of $2024$; if the first is even, the second must be one of $1011$ evens. So
$$P = \frac{1013}{2025}\cdot\frac{1012}{2024} + \frac{1012}{2025}\cdot\frac{1011}{2024} = \frac{1012(1013 + 1011)}{2025 \cdot 2024} = \frac{1012}{2025}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{1012}{2025}$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-26.title: Find the number of songs
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-26.body:
In seconds: with $n$ songs originally, $179n + 170 = 178(n + 1)$, so $n = 8$. The total is now $179 \cdot 8 + 170 + 1016 = 2618$ seconds over $14$ songs, an average of $\frac{2618}{14} = 187$ seconds.

**Answer: 187**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-26.title: Think in deviations
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-26.body:
Measure songs relative to $178$ s. The original $n$ songs are each $+1$ on average and the new song is $-8$; for the new average to be exactly $178$, $n - 8 = 0$, so $n = 8$ and the $9$ songs total $9 \cdot 178 = 1602$ s. The five extra songs total $1016$ s, so the average is $\frac{1602 + 1016}{14} = \frac{2618}{14} = 187$ s.

**Answer: 187**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-27.title: Compare bases with the same height
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-27.body:
$ABCE$ and $BADF$ are parallelograms, so $EC = DF = AB = 7$ and $EF = 17 - 7 - 7 = 3$. Quadrilateral $ABEF$ is a trapezoid with bases $7$ and $3$ and the same height $h$ as $ABCD$. From $\frac{7 + 17}{2}h = 588$, $h = 49$, so
$$[ABEF] = \frac{7 + 3}{2}\cdot 49 = 245.$$

**Answer: 245**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-27.title: Ratio of base sums
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-27.body:
Since the two trapezoids share the height, their areas are in the ratio of their base sums: $[ABEF] = \frac{7 + 3}{7 + 17}\cdot 588 = \frac{5}{12} \cdot 588 = 245$. (In general the answer is $\frac{b - a}{b + a}[ABCD]$ for bases $a < b$.)

**Answer: 245**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-28.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-28.body:
$2024 = 8 \cdot 11 \cdot 23$; handle each prime power.
- **Mod 8:** $n$ must be odd (else $n^{22} - 1$ is odd), and every odd $n$ has $n^2 \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, so $n^{22} \equiv 1$. That's $4$ residues.
- **Mod 11:** if $11 \nmid n$, Fermat gives $n^{10} \equiv 1$, so $n^{22} \equiv n^2$; we need $n^2 \equiv 1$, i.e. $n \equiv \pm 1$: $2$ residues.
- **Mod 23:** Fermat gives $n^{22} \equiv 1$ for all $n \not\equiv 0$: $22$ residues.

By CRT each combination of residues corresponds to exactly one $n \in [1, 2024]$, so there are $4 \cdot 2 \cdot 22 = 176$ values.

**Answer: 176**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-28.title: Group-theoretic count
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-28.body:
The condition says $n$ is a unit mod $2024$ whose order divides $22$. The unit group is $(\mathbb{Z}/8)^\times \times (\mathbb{Z}/11)^\times \times (\mathbb{Z}/23)^\times \cong C_2^2 \times C_{10} \times C_{22}$. The number of elements with $x^{22} = 1$ in a cyclic group $C_m$ is $\gcd(22, m)$: this gives $2 \cdot 2 = 4$, $\gcd(22,10) = 2$ and $\gcd(22, 22) = 22$, for $4 \cdot 2 \cdot 22 = 176$. A direct computer check over $n \le 2024$ agrees.

**Answer: 176**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-29.title: Factor
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-29.body:
$y \ne 0$. From $xy = \frac{x}{y}$: $x(y^2 - 1) = 0$, so $x = 0$ or $y = \pm 1$.
- $x = 0$: then $y = 0$, impossible.
- $y = 1$: $x + 1 = x$, impossible.
- $y = -1$: $x - 1 = -x$, so $x = \frac12$. Check: $x + y = -\frac12$, $xy = -\frac12$, $\frac xy = -\frac12$. ✓

So $x - y = \frac12 + 1 = \frac32$.

**Answer: $\frac32$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-29.title: Divide first
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-29.body:
If $x = 0$ then $y = 0$, which is not allowed, so $x \ne 0$ and $xy = \frac xy$ gives $y^2 = 1$. Then $x + y = xy$ means $x(1 - y) = -y$. With $y = 1$ this reads $0 = -1$ (no), and with $y = -1$ it reads $2x = 1$, so $x = \frac12$ and $x - y = \frac32$.

**Answer: $\frac32$**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-30.title: Each row has two of each color
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-30.body:
Think of $6$ rows (fixed $y$) of $4$ points each. A monochromatic rectangle appears exactly when two rows share two positions of the same color.

**Lemma:** no row can have $3$ or more points of one color. Suppose a row has red at positions $1, 2, 3$. Every other row has at most one red among positions $1,2,3$ (else a red rectangle), so its pattern on those positions is one of RBB, BRB, BBR, BBB, and two rows can't share a pattern (each pattern has two equal colors in the same places). That allows at most $4$ other rows, but we need $5$. Contradiction.

So every row has exactly two red and two blue points: one of the $\binom42 = 6$ patterns RRBB, RBRB, RBBR, BRRB, BRBR, BBRR. Two equal rows would form a rectangle, so all six patterns appear once each. Any two different patterns share at most one red and at most one blue position (they share a red pair only if they are equal; a shared blue pair forces the same red pair). So every arrangement works, and there are $6! = 720$ of them.

**Answer: 720**

nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-30.title: Computer check
nyciml-2024-25-fall-seniora-30.body:
Encode each row as a 4-bit mask of red points. A coloring is valid iff for every two rows the masks share at most one red bit and at most one blue bit. Checking all $16^6$ assignments of masks gives exactly $720$ valid colorings, matching the argument (each valid coloring uses the six two-red patterns once each).

**Answer: 720**
